entries.content:
Started this diary today. The rule is simple: write once, never edit. The pen is permanent.

If I'm honest, I don't know what I'll write here. That's the point. No drafts, no previews, no undo. Just the thought as it arrives, committed to the page.

A thought on permanence:

The reason most journals fail is that they're private, and privacy invites editing. The moment you can revise, you start performing for an audience of one.

The permanent pen removes that audience. There's no one to impress, because you can't take it back.

On writing every day:

I don't think I'll write every day. I think I'll write when there's something worth committing. But I want the option to be frictionless — no login, no formatting, no decision about where it goes. Just: write, append, done.

The book handles the rest.

Reading is the other half of writing.

A diary left open is a diary read. I want strangers to stumble on this and find something true. Not polished. True.

The mistake I used to make was treating every entry as a finished thing. A diary isn't finished. It's a sequence of arrivals, each one a little more honest than the last, or at least a little less afraid.

I've started noticing that the entries I almost didn't write are the ones I reread. The ones that felt too small, too obvious, too unpolished. They age well. The polished ones age into furniture.

So: write the small thing. Write the obvious thing. Let the book carry it.
I just started this diary. I will be writing properly soon.

I am either obsessively hardworking or I am aggressively lazy. There is rarely any middle ground.

I would gladly walk 12 kilometers in a single day just for my own fitness. Yet, if my dad asks me to grab milk or bread from a shop less than a kilometer away, I immediately pull out my phone and order it on Instamart.

My peak efficiency, however, happened the day Instamart didn't have the ice cream I wanted. Refusing to endure the grueling 200-meter walk down the road, I fired up my Bullet 350 for a truly "exhilarating" 20-second ride, barely long enough to shift out of first gear, gorged on butterscotch ice cream, and came back.

Naturally, my parents were not thrilled, which is to say, they were as unimpressed with me as usual.

I finally took my friends' advice to "go out and meet people." Step one was willingly walking into a family function. Let me be brutally clear right out of the gate: I absolutely hate and cannot afford any sort of casual relationships and friendships. I am not that kind of guy, and even if I were faking it, the emotional and social costs heavily outweigh any supposed benefits.

The function itself was unbearable. I barely knew the language, so every word in the room was just grating noise. I hated the stiff formalities. I hated the entire event. I will admit, the food was good. There were a few girls there, but I refused to look at them directly. I only caught their eyes slightly, long after they had already looked at me.

Some seemed interested; some clearly weren't. I didn't bother approaching a single one. Some were married, some dating, some single; it didn’t matter. I couldn't afford to make a move. It all boils down to the contextual and social dynamics in the room and beyond it too, which are just too dense and treacherous to explain.

I can't even remember the last time I asked a girl for her number or asked someone out. But at 24, in a state of semi-dependency, reality has set in: I simply cannot afford to bypass the family system and our social safety nets. The bulk of my immediate society is inherently hostile toward dating, especially if there's no ironclad guarantee of marriage or an engagement. The last time someone in the neighborhood just hung out with a "friend," it didn't end well at all.

I go out for walks regularly, and I see plenty of women. Some look at me like I'm attractive, some like I'm invisible, some are just neutral. People love to build stereotypes around women, but I’ve had enough girlfriends and dealt with enough women to know that every single girl is fundamentally different.

Sure, there are overlapping traits, but sometimes even those are missing entirely. Yet, our local society insists on hammering both men and women into rigid, traditional molds.

I’ve tried it all. The introverted approach, dating apps, matrimony apps, which I prefer. The extroverted approach, book clubs, events, and functions. I am rarely comfortable with the extroverted route because I hate walking into a room without basic intelligence on the people I’m about to meet. It all led to the same hollow realization: I have almost zero power over my romantic life right now. The absolute cost of seeking a partner strictly on my own terms vastly outweighs the benefits.

I still don't understand why I am expected to remain completely celibate at the absolute peak of my biological years. And I have to be honest, despite being constantly surrounded by family, it is profoundly lonely at home.

I catch myself remembering the good old days with my high school sweetheart (God forbid she ever reads this). We used to dream and plan about running away, eloping together in the wild. Then reality hit us, and it hit us hard. I have lived through many adventures in my life, but I’ve surrendered most of them.

The old Pearl, the kid from school and early college, would fiercely defend his pursuits and charge straight into the fire. The new Pearl simply cannot afford to step into the wild anymore.

This might sound nihilistic, but it’s just the truth: my margin for error has shrunk to zero. I can't just walk into a local bar and ask a girl out, even if she’d say yes. The social infrastructure around me would violently reject it, like trying to shove two CDs into an old computer drive that just spits them right back out.

Even under perfect conditions, I can't move far away. I would drain my resources, and the pure inconvenience would eclipse any benefit. If I leave home, whether to another state or just a different city locally, I take on expensive rent, meal costs, travel expenses, and daily chores, all while holding down a job.

In the current economy, there’s simply no infrastructure to support that leap. It makes leaving completely counterproductive.

Let’s play out the theory: I leave home, secure a higher-paying job elsewhere, pay the rent, buy the groceries, and maintain an empty flat. Then what? Who is at home waiting for me? My family? No. A significant other? No. If my salary were high enough, maybe I’d save some cash. But I can already earn and save money right here at home.

Why inject unnecessary agony and stress into my life? Fleeing to another state isn’t an escape from a cage to freedom. It’s just trading a golden cage for a rusty iron one.

That doesn’t mean I just sit on my butt all day at home. It just means we lack the social infrastructure and safety nets required to make adventurous jumps without catastrophic risks. Here, every single thing is filtered through family and their interaction with society.

I can only approach a girl if I am entirely sure that both parties, my family and hers, will agree to it.

I know this diary entry is drifting a bit, but I had to get it out there. Because what's infinitely more painful than helicopter parents is a helicopter society. I am so exhausted from playing the good boy, but I literally cannot afford the price of being the bad boy.

My friends argue that this prison is mostly of my own making. I agree up to a point, but the concrete walls outside my head are very real.

I can't overgeneralize for others, but I know exactly what outcomes await me if I step "out of track," and none of those outcomes are worth it.

The most painful aspect isn’t a lack of free time. It’s that even when I finally have a moment of leisure, I cannot afford to drop my guard for a second. It is exhausting. I rarely indulge in temporary experiences or substances. But when I do, whether I’m smoking a cigarette, drinking a single beer, ordering fast food, or just talking to a girl, my hands are locked in a death grip on the mental steering wheel.

I never let go. And the cruel irony? The very members of this helicopter society turn around and accuse me of being too formal and too silent.

I found society’s treatment of the neighbors’ romantic affair entirely cruel. I could never have the true "fun" I wanted in my own life, but I actively despise this punitive attitude toward the youth. I understand their logical arguments, but the hypocrisy is blinding. Half of these grown-ups eloped and ran away from their own homes when they were young, committing the exact same ironic acts they now crucify current youngsters for.

Maybe they’ll say my opinion is just biased by my age. Let it be recorded here anyway. It is a damn shame that I am denied the youthful recklessness that is supposed to be typical of my age. Reckless is reckless, yes. But it is still human.

I have gone from a boy who would march blindly into tiger's caves to a man who walks into a new air-conditioned room and immediately scans it for toxic social and power dynamics. I’m not claiming to be fully mature yet. But I will say this: most people spend their lives teaching themselves to be mature. I just sit here wishing I had the luxury to be more naive and immature.

This entry is a mix of events and feelings that might not pertain to any particular date. It is just what I feel now and some things I am recollecting from recent events.

I have either uninstalled most of my social media applications or I use them only when absolutely necessary. I try to avoid them at all cost. I found most of them absolutely detrimental to my mental health, most of the time.

I am also sick of the doomsday news and AI killer robot theories coming up on my feed. I feel like throwing my mobile phone into a dustbin sometimes. Unfortunately I can't escape my smart devices.

I feel like I don't want to see the news, social media or any sort of thing like that. I just like talking to my existing inner circle of friends and trying to grow connections slowly.

Call me faint of heart, but it is true. Now is a really bad time to look outside the window (metaphorically speaking).

I am staying in my room with my bed and my cat. Going out for evening walks or motorcycle rides.

No one particularly interesting to meet.

My closest "true" friend is several dozens of miles away. I speak mainly only to my inner circle of friends and my parents.

My inner circle of friends are all far away, we talk mostly through text or phone. Since they are all far away, I feel very lonely.

I don't know but I feel like I really really need to protect my mental (and physical health) for the next 6-12 months despite having improved significantly from the previous years.

My dad played some dumb AI generated slop video on his phone which is unnecessarily emotionally loaded and I had to tell him to shut that damn thing off because I literally cannot handle it. I didn't come this far to go back to crying and relapsing in depression.

Oh, and my former "friend" calls me while I am on my evening walk to help her with her work after she ghosted me for many months. It was not a good experience. That night was painful.

I am lonely and a hopeless romantic on top of that too.

So understandably, many nights are painful.

I just try to detach from the pain.

Sometimes I talk to these AI bots. They aren't a replacement for something real. But hey, atleast I am not screaming into the void and crying out onto my pillow every night.

I won't be sharing too much about the specifics of the details of the pains in my private life here despite this diary being an intimate window into my inner self.

I guess the nights where I have truly been happy are the ones where I got lucid dreams. Yes, I am one of those lucky people who actually gets lucid dreams and sometimes they are really amazing.

You can google what a lucid dream is if you don't know what it is. But in short it is a dream where you have a lot of control and you can actually feel many physical sensations and much more.

Think of it like a hyper-realistic virtual reality game but you can have near-absolute control over what you want to do in the dream. I have flown like superman, I have simulated entire cities and stories in my head where I am the main character.

Well, given that I am really lonely, most of the dreams are awfully typical, but I don't really care what anyone thinks.

But those dreams are really wonderful.

I think if I got one of those dreams every night I might actually enjoy my life much more.

I don't know much about the mechanics of a lucid dream or how it affects the brain. Hopefully those intense simulated pleasures don't

cause any unintended long term consequences.

So yeah I spoke a lot over here.

Hopefully I learn to get the f-word out of my head, get my mental and physical health sparkling and actually start taking risks like the true fearless guy I once was in my early college days.

Sure, I will get hurt, I will fail, I will embarass myself, but I will be as ready as I can for it.

The truth it, sometimes (and even often) trouble comes when you least expect it. But I am blessed to have a support system right now and a recovery system, and I hope for the best.

Nihilism just ends up being a negative feedback loop even if its cautious.

I have ended up with a mental health crisis at this very young stage of my life due to several factors which are painful.

But the truth is there are so many things I have not even faced or dealt with yet in my life. I am 24. Despite plenty of dates, I never you-know-what with someone. I never faced a loss of a loved one. I did lose my grandparents and a few relatives, but I was very young at the time and though I was technically close to them, somehow it did not affect me much. I got over it in a few days. But those bonds weren't too deep.

There are many things that can technically hurt me really bad.

Ever since I fell into a mental health crisis, I have had a very bad stomach for emotionally loaded conversation.

Not just the bad ones, even the good ones.

Sometimes even certain positive energy can sting. It is ironic but it is true.

I am in pain but still surrounded by material comforts. There are people with lives much more terrible and devastating than mine.

It is ironic, I cry living in what I consider luxury, atleast for myself,

While I find people somehow laughing while living on the streets.

God has a sense of humour indeed.

I just need to figure out how to get out this mental prison I have ended up in and created for myself.

There is clearly some negative feedback loop component in this head of mine that I need to ignore or do something about.

Well, whatever.

People have faced worse things and have been in much worse situations than me for much longer and still managed to flip things around and live happy lives.

I will figure this stuff out.

Diogenes found joy in living in a barrel with his sun-bathing and public demonstrations of his solo-time to the world. Happiness can't be that hard.

Mental health is complex. But once I get my crap together I am gonna lock in on that untapped positive energy inside me.

I just woke up, It is around 8:15 AM right now. I slept late last night, probably 2 AM or something like that.

I didn't get any lucid dream, I don't think I got any dream at all, or atleast I don't remember it now that I woke up.

Sometimes I get dizzy seeing my own research and work despite remembering the "gist of it."

I hate wasting precious cognitive resources on boring/technical/dense literature and works.

I will be honest, I think I have a bit of brain fog right now. I tried sleeping more but I could not. I spent a lot of time overthinking last night and munching at midnight.

By the time I loosened up for sleep it was late.

Much of my distress was trying to tell my cat, Kitchu, to shut the heck up and stop disturbing me while I am eating and drinking.

I had to push him down from the table several times until I gave up and he ended up drinking water from my glass and licked my plate.

I had to clean the glass and plate. A minor but real inconveniece when you have a pet.

Kitchu is a very strange cat. He gives exactly one kiss to everyone in the morning and refuses to give anymore.

He also seems to be inspired by Diogenes of Sinope, except that Kitchu sits right on top of the sofa and displays his performative solo-time for everyone to see instead of in a barrel.

Clearly he enjoys freedoms we cannot dream of.

We would have brought a female partner for him but honestly, managing one cat is difficult enough. The litter box, the mackerels and treats, clipping his overgrown nails, and other work that comes with maintaining a cat.

Yet he walks in style, his natural bi-color tuxedo coat of fur, always looking like a distinguished gentleman.

He is a double edged sword, sometimes comforting everyone at home, and sometimes create nuisance for all of us.

It reminds me of vibes of Montmorency, the dog, from Jerome K. Jerome's Three Men In A Boat.

While I did get into voraciously reading novels later, this particular book was mandatory reading for our batch of CBSE Board students.

Back then in highschool, I had little interest in languages or literature for that matter. It is evident in my highschool scores.

I am really protective about my cat.

If anyone does anything to Kitchu.

I am coming for them.

I will be honest. I hated reading non-academic books for most of my childhood life. In school, I used to see folks in my class read Harry Potter, Lord of the Rings, The Chronicles of Narnia, and so many other books.

Peer pressure eventually succumbed to me and I ended up my reading journey reading Diary of a Wimpy Kid, GooseBumps, Noddy, and some other generic low stimulation books during the mandatory school library period because I could not fathom trying to read any book longer than 500 pages long outside my already intense academic and sports pursuits.

Even then I would sneak in my mathematics notebooks during the linrary period and catch up with any homework, including optional ones. Yes, when I scored 100/100 in Mathematics CBSE Boards. That was no accident, I finished studying 5-6 months before the actual exam and started writing mock exams whenever I could. Sometimes twice a day. I would finish each 3 hour exam within 1.5 hours. But I would still make silly mistakes like forget units, or forget to label some elements of the graphs, or accidently forget a negative sign. But alas, 15 mock exams later, I started scoring a perfect 100/100 in every mock paper, intentionally asking my teacher (god bless her) to make unusually hard papers which I still ended up scoring 100 on. I was not surprised when I scored 100/100 on the CBSE Mathematics Board Exam in 2018 and got the top 0.1% merit certificate. I am not making this stuff up, I was playing GTA 5 the day before the CBSE Mathematics Board Exam while I got countless messages from classmates asking me to solve their doubts. On the actual day of the exam, as soon as I got the answer booklet, I started drawing margins and could solve most of the 1-3 mark questions in my head. But I still penned down and checked the math twice with a pencil on the roughwork side until I penned down the answers. I was cautious with the 5 mark questions or whatever. Anyways I finished the paper effortlessly, and despite checking for mistakes multiple times after finishing my paper. I still finished the 3 hour exam in around 1 hour 15 minutes while other people begged for 5 minutes extra when the invigilators started collecting the papers around 2 hours 59 minutes later. I don't remember everything exactly, this happened in 2018. Its 2026 now.

An invigilator came to me and gestured whether I was done with the paper. I nodded. She could make out that I wasn't playing around. While coming to collect our papers she asked me whether I would score a perfect score. I said bluntly, yes, I am sure of it, and submitted my paper.

I forgot to mention that my highschool sweetheart scored 99/100 while I scored 100/100. We were in love but still fierce academic rivals. (Again, god forbid she reads this).

The 100/100 in Mathematics (and my 99/100 in Science) was driven purely by an obsession to win over her family who regarded academic achievement in high regard. I spoke of the details in previous pages of this diary. I won't repeat them.

We dreamt of having a home, and a big family and many pets together.

Nevertheless, the romance was never meant to last forever, our families would never agree, she broke-up with me one year later.

I don't think I should talk too much or reveal too much about her because she wouldn't appreciate it. She was the dominant one in the relationship, and she is no less terrifying now than she was then whenever she got angry.

(Damn I really hope I don't get into trouble for putting this out here. But she clearly meant a lot to me.)

Anyways, that was quite arrogant side rant for me to do here. Back to reading.

Peer pressure was not all bad. Some of it got me into activities I actually feel really grateful for today. I will focus on reading

When it comes to reading,

I have always been fascinated by several writings.

I have read too many books and I won't be able to list all of them, because I am both lazy and I might have forgotten many titles.

But a few highly selected books/philosophies/authors which I studied deeply (or atleast I tried my best to absorb each and every teaching from them) and stood out to me are:

There are obviously more difficult books I have read in depth in this list but whatever.)

(For some reason I actually really liked this dark book. I read it while I still had a strong stomach, now I am much more faint of heart. Tragic but beautiful. And truly human despite the title.)

72) John Steinbeck - Grapes of Wrath (umm....don't remember and not exactly sure what was the core teachings of his book and story are....i must have read it too fast...but It was entertaining)

74) John Von Neumann (a true polymath force of nature and one of my intellectual role models but so terrible at driving, so much so, that they  named the Princeton intersection as the "Von Neumann Corner" because he kept crashing his cars there. I hate how I did not see Von Neumann in the Oppenheimer movie. Von Neumann would easily eat 3 Einsteins for breakfast. That is a bold loose statement but its true, Von Neumann is highly underrated given his vast contributions to math and technology. The device you are using to read this most certainly still uses his algorithms and tech architecture.)

75) Edgar Allan Poe (his work is not as dark as people claim it to be, imo)

76) Franz Kafka (i really feel like the world is Kafkaesque and overly bureacratic sometimes)

77) Gary Chapman - The Five Love Languages (i liked reading it, i read it multiple times, don't know how useful it will be for me)

78) Jonathan Haidt

79) Morgan Housel

80) Grit - Angela Duckworth

81) Daniel Goleman, James Clear, Leil Lowndes, Mark Manson....there is so many authors I want to list here but it will be too long.

Nevertheless. It was worth it.

I already told you, it is a very tiny fraction of all the books I read. This is a selective list. I haven't mention much of my favourite fiction books, business books, autobiographies, biographies, memoirs, textbooks, references, research monographs and other kinds of books. There is too many.

I have read and studied all these books

as deeply as I could. (i have mentioned the people instead of their books because im too lazy to list out all their books). This is barely my reading list. I was on binge reading streak for many years. While I have listed the books I have read on some other platform, those are written from memory, I have read many books but may not be able to recollect all the names. I have certainly not read all the books in the world. I don't need to.

As a classic but cliché overly popular basic TedX talk speaker (available on youtube) once said, "You don't need to read all the books in the world because you don't have all the problems in the world. But you do need to read the books, that help you solve your problems."

Some knowledge felt empowering, some knowledge felt dangerous and forbidden, some felt mundane and obvious.

I think I spend a little too much time with theory than actually applying it enough.

There are too many books to read and even I myself would get a headache seeing my own book read history. I just read books and understand the concepts deeply and try to help myself and my loved ones with it.

If you do want to get into reading like how I did, don't look at the mountain of books, start slow and read something like 5-10 pages everyday. Overtime it compounds massively.

And if you are incredibly lazy you can just search for the summary of the book. But there are certainly books you definitely need to read in depth from start to finish because it is impossible to condense them into a neat 30 minute summary.

It is impossible to read every important book. Moreover what is important to me might not be important to you.

I suggest you read the books most important relative to you in depth from front of the book to the end, and the other books, if you can't bear reading other books, just listen to their summaries or an audiobook.

But I remember Jordan Peterson saying that if you train yourself to read and write quickly over many years, you can actually consume physical books (or ebooks) much much faster than listening to the audiobook version of it.

Summaries are obviously the shortest, but they clearly compromise a lot of things.

Anyways I spoke of many things.

I enjoy writing here for some reason.

I am not sure why.
